topic: A job offer from the library
context: You live near the local library and you are currently unemployed. You received an email from the library manager offering you a job.

paragraphs: As we have expanded the library, we are looking for a hard-working person to join our team.

We have been told that you are not working at the moment and that you have some experience of working in a library, so we are contacting you. What do you think about working with us? We appreciate your opinion very much.

task11: Write a letter to your friend. Tell them about this job offer. Write about your feelings and whether you will accept the offer.
task12: Write a letter to the manager. Write about your feelings and whether you accept the offer.
part2_question: Should children learn a foreign language from the time they start school, or is it better to wait until secondary school?

task11: You will never guess what happened. The library down the road has offered me a job! I am delighted, especially after months of looking. The work suits my experience and it is five minutes from home, so I am going to accept. Let us celebrate at the weekend.
task12: Thank you very much for your email offering me a position on the library team. I was delighted to receive it, and I am pleased that my earlier experience in a library has been remembered.

I am happy to accept the offer. The work appeals to me a great deal: I enjoy helping readers find what they need, and I would welcome the chance to contribute to the library as it expands. I am also familiar with the cataloguing system you use, which should allow me to be useful from the first week.
I am available to start at short notice and would be glad to meet you to discuss hours, duties and any training involved. Please let me know a time that suits you.
part2: This is a long-running debate, and although both approaches have something to recommend them, I am firmly in favour of starting early.

The main argument for primary school is that young children are extraordinarily receptive to new sounds and patterns. They absorb pronunciation without effort and, crucially, they are not yet self-conscious enough to be afraid of making mistakes, which is precisely what fluency requires. Children who begin Spanish at six usually end up with a more natural accent and a surer instinct for grammar than those who begin at twelve.

I do accept, however, that starting early is only useful if it is done well. Formal grammar drills with seven-year-olds achieve very little and can put a child off the language for years. Early teaching has to be built on songs, games and stories. The same is true of listening: a young ear distinguishes unfamiliar sounds that an adult learner may never hear properly at all.
Provided primary schools can offer that kind of lively, immersive teaching, I believe starting young gives children a lasting advantage and a skill they will keep for life.
